One rule before we start: every number here comes from my own Usage page. Viktor runs on what I set. He doesn't choose a model for each job by himself, and nothing changed without my yes.

> Don’t let one part of the app import from another: lock it with folders, not even types can cross

> Don’t make agents handle the hard parts: hide them behind simple APIs, like their framework Dune

> Don’t add another line to AGENTS.md: turn every correction into a lint rule

The result: her team merged 11,000 PRs in October, and only 0.47% got reverted

I Folded a Whole Research Pipeline Into One Folder and Let the Agents Run It

A build log. Every number below comes from a 659k-view guide to agent swarms and from the studies it cites. I ran the same pattern on a smaller job and kept the structure.
OpenAI pointed about 10,000 agents at a Navier-Stokes claim in September. 88 hours later they had a proposed answer. Mathematicians are still disputing it.
You cannot replicate that width on a laptop. But the architecture scales down to a single directory. One agent carves up the job, several handle the pieces in parallel, a clean agent grades every result, and the original agent stitches the survivors into one deliverable.
My early draft of this loop was terrible. No rules, no checker, no discipline around who writes which file. Everything that could break did break. What follows is the fixed version: 7 rules, 4 roles, 9 files, and the admission that made me rebuild the whole thing.
 
The shape of the swarm
 
Four roles and nothing else.
The lead reads BOARD.md, reads the last cycle's LESSONS.md, and writes one brief per piece of the big job.
Workers each accept a single brief, produce a single output file, and leave everything else untouched.

virals.text:
I've been talking to a bunch of PhD students and researchers recently, and I've qualitatively noticed two growing (but concerning) trends with AI:

1. Researchers seem to be reading less. Some even reported that they read <10 papers a year now with AI because they can simply either 1) retrieve or 2) summarize papers. BUT deep reading is how we engage with underlying intellectual arguments, develop research taste, spot methodological flaws, and form original ideas. It's arguably the most fun part of a PhD imo

2. Researchers seem to be vibe-coding and paper-maxxing. AI dramatically cheapens execution, such as implementing experiments, running analyses, and producing manuscripts. Some even "let [Claude Code] rip" without checking the code or validating the results somehow. BUT it also incentivizes quantity over depth, rigor, and meaningful contributions.

Overall, the cost of producing research is falling much faster than the cost of developing genuine intellectual understanding. Rather than simply producing more papers, I think we should engage deeply with the literature, ask questions that truly matter, and produce work that meaningfully advances our collective understanding.

virals.text:
Jensen Huang asked for his job back this week, and Nvidia's board said no within a few hours.

The guy who turned Nvidia into the first $5 trillion company in history has roughly half as many votes there as Vanguard.

Here's how that happens. Nvidia runs on one share, one vote. Jensen owns about 3.5% of the company. That makes him the largest individual shareholder, with exactly one vote per share, same as anybody else. Vanguard and BlackRock each own more than 7%.

Meta works differently. Zuckerberg owns about 13% of it, but his shares carry 10 votes each, so he controls around 60% of the vote and can pick the whole board himself. Larry and Sergey still have majority control of Alphabet years after they stepped back from running it.

Nvidia went public in 1999, five years before Google's IPO made super-voting founder shares a normal thing in Silicon Valley. Nvidia never switched. Its bylaws let the board remove the CEO for any reason, at any time.

The timing made it sting even more. The same earnings call where the board shut the door showed $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year ago. That quarter ran August through October, so every dollar of it came in with Jensen in charge.

To be fair to the board, they do have real reasons to wait. Wachtell Lipton is still investigating his relationship with a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset. The SEC is reportedly looking at whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. And the Treasury Secretary went on TV asking whether Nvidia chips got into China through Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought more than $4 billion of them and denies diverting any. If a director votes to bring Jensen back before those answers come in, whatever turns up later lands on that director.

That's also why Colette Kress sounds so stiff in this clip. She's signed off on Nvidia's financials as CFO since 2013, and now the SEC is going through them. You don't ad-lib on Mad Money in that spot.

Back in January, Jensen said on a podcast that the CEO was always supposed to answer to the board. He started this company in a Denny's booth, took it to $5 trillion, and the whole way up he never had more votes per share than someone holding NVDA in a Robinhood account.

Anthropic's Claude Code team just explained why Claude codes better when it verifies its work.

The ClaudeDevs account posted today that Claude writes better code when it can check its own output. Tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs used to be expensive. Now they are cheap. The post links a https://t.co/5aqwkNYwDR blog on how the Claude Code team thinks about verification. It has 365.8K views, 6.8K reposts and 7.5K likes so far.

The timing matters. Claude Fable 5.2 launched November 9 alongside Mythos 5.2, and developers are now judging it on coding and long-running agent work. Anthropic's launch post says Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1% at Xhigh effort, the highest score of any released model it has tested. At High effort it scores 45.3%, about level with Opus 5.5's best of 45.5%, for roughly half the cost per task. One third-party test, KingBench, had it at 70% against Opus 5.5's 57.8% on coding.

Developer reaction is split. Theo calls it weird but incredible. Another developer says it is expensive, ignores instructions and is weak at AI research, with frontend its best area, and rates Opus better elsewhere. Others say it needs no extra skills or workflows, just the task. Artificial Analysis finds it more direct than Fable 5.1, with shorter answers and almost no em dashes, but lower on informativeness and conviction.

Key numbers:
- Price: $8 per million input tokens, $40 per million output tokens
- Context window: 1M tokens, max output 128K tokens
- Input: text and images
- Claude Code: v2.1.321 or later, run /model fable
- Also live on NEAR AI Cloud, with a free playground

The takeaway: Anthropic is pitching cheap verification as the reason Fable 5.2 does well on agent and coding tasks.

outsiders.name: Hayoung Jung
outsiders.text:
I've been talking to a bunch of PhD students and researchers recently, and I've qualitatively noticed two growing (but concerning) trends with AI:

1. Researchers seem to be reading less. Some even reported that they read <10 papers a year now with AI because they can simply either 1) retrieve or 2) summarize papers. BUT deep reading is how we engage with underlying intellectual arguments, develop research taste, spot methodological flaws, and form original ideas. It's arguably the most fun part of a PhD imo

2. Researchers seem to be vibe-coding and paper-maxxing. AI dramatically cheapens execution, such as implementing experiments, running analyses, and producing manuscripts. Some even "let [Claude Code] rip" without checking the code or validating the results somehow. BUT it also incentivizes quantity over depth, rigor, and meaningful contributions.

Overall, the cost of producing research is falling much faster than the cost of developing genuine intellectual understanding. Rather than simply producing more papers, I think we should engage deeply with the literature, ask questions that truly matter, and produce work that meaningfully advances our collective understanding.

outsiders.text:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: keep Opus 5.5 as your main model, and put Fable 5.2 on call as the advisor that checks its biggest decisions.

Fable 5.2 beat Opus 5.5 on FrontierSWE v2, 69.9% to 62.3%. You don't have to move your whole session to Fable to get that edge, it only steps in where the outcome is decided.

You just start Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --advisor fable

this is how it splits:

→ Opus 5.5 runs the session and writes the code like it always does
→ Haiku 5.5 subagents search the repo and run the tests in parallel
→ Fable 5.2 reads the full transcript only at the decision points
→ Opus keeps its speed, Fable adds a second opinion from a stronger model

Fable only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan gets locked
→ when the same error comes back twice
→ before Claude calls the task done

Opus works. Haiku digs. Fable checks.

JEV engineering is the same idea one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) get settled by JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the main session and edits the code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds every call site on Haiku 5.5
> test-runner runs the suite on Haiku 5.5 and reports only failures
> Fable 5.2 on call as advisor, reads the full transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 with Fable 5.2 as advisor.
2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), test-runner (runs the suite, reports only failures).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before a plan locks, after the same error twice, and before a task is marked done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. Nothing gets edited until I say go."

Opus 5.5 accepts Fable as its advisor, it's in the docs pairing table. needs Fable access. run claude update, then /model fable once if your plan bills Fable to usage credits.

↳ https://t.co/vOifNVjYxB

save it, even Opus deserves a second opinion.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
Jensen Huang asked for his job back this week, and Nvidia's board said no within a few hours.

The guy who turned Nvidia into the first $5 trillion company in history has roughly half as many votes there as Vanguard.

Here's how that happens. Nvidia runs on one share, one vote. Jensen owns about 3.5% of the company. That makes him the largest individual shareholder, with exactly one vote per share, same as anybody else. Vanguard and BlackRock each own more than 7%.

Meta works differently. Zuckerberg owns about 13% of it, but his shares carry 10 votes each, so he controls around 60% of the vote and can pick the whole board himself. Larry and Sergey still have majority control of Alphabet years after they stepped back from running it.

Nvidia went public in 1999, five years before Google's IPO made super-voting founder shares a normal thing in Silicon Valley. Nvidia never switched. Its bylaws let the board remove the CEO for any reason, at any time.

The timing made it sting even more. The same earnings call where the board shut the door showed $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year ago. That quarter ran August through October, so every dollar of it came in with Jensen in charge.

To be fair to the board, they do have real reasons to wait. Wachtell Lipton is still investigating his relationship with a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset. The SEC is reportedly looking at whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. And the Treasury Secretary went on TV asking whether Nvidia chips got into China through Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought more than $4 billion of them and denies diverting any. If a director votes to bring Jensen back before those answers come in, whatever turns up later lands on that director.

That's also why Colette Kress sounds so stiff in this clip. She's signed off on Nvidia's financials as CFO since 2013, and now the SEC is going through them. You don't ad-lib on Mad Money in that spot.

Back in January, Jensen said on a podcast that the CEO was always supposed to answer to the board. He started this company in a Denny's booth, took it to $5 trillion, and the whole way up he never had more votes per share than someone holding NVDA in a Robinhood account.

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Reconfigure my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

outsiders.text:
Anthropic's Claude Code team just explained why Claude codes better when it verifies its work.

The ClaudeDevs account posted today that Claude writes better code when it can check its own output. Tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs used to be expensive. Now they are cheap. The post links a https://t.co/5aqwkNYwDR blog on how the Claude Code team thinks about verification. It has 365.8K views, 6.8K reposts and 7.5K likes so far.

The timing matters. Claude Fable 5.2 launched November 9 alongside Mythos 5.2, and developers are now judging it on coding and long-running agent work. Anthropic's launch post says Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1% at Xhigh effort, the highest score of any released model it has tested. At High effort it scores 45.3%, about level with Opus 5.5's best of 45.5%, for roughly half the cost per task. One third-party test, KingBench, had it at 70% against Opus 5.5's 57.8% on coding.

Developer reaction is split. Theo calls it weird but incredible. Another developer says it is expensive, ignores instructions and is weak at AI research, with frontend its best area, and rates Opus better elsewhere. Others say it needs no extra skills or workflows, just the task. Artificial Analysis finds it more direct than Fable 5.1, with shorter answers and almost no em dashes, but lower on informativeness and conviction.

Key numbers:
- Price: $8 per million input tokens, $40 per million output tokens
- Context window: 1M tokens, max output 128K tokens
- Input: text and images
- Claude Code: v2.1.321 or later, run /model fable
- Also live on NEAR AI Cloud, with a free playground

The takeaway: Anthropic is pitching cheap verification as the reason Fable 5.2 does well on agent and coding tasks.
